questions.stem: A 73-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of progressive, pruritic lesions primarily on his legs. He had a history of uncontrolled asthma and had taken oral prednisone multiple times in the preceding 4 months. On examination:
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Crusted scabies The correct answer is crusted scabies. While scabies can affect anyone, groups of people at higher risk for crusted scabies include the elderly, those with a psychiatric disorder or intellectual disability, HTLV-1 infection, and patients who are immunosuppressed (HIV/AIDS, diabetes, steroid use, etc.). Scabies typically involves dozens of mites that cause itching nodules and burrows primarily in the trunk/extremities, genital areas, web spaces, and wrists/ankles. In crusted scabies, thousands to millions of mites cause itching (50% of cases), lesions may involve the whole body and include crusting (see feet in picture) and may present as erythroderma (like the lesions in the more proximal lower extremity in the picture). Treatment of crusted scabies requires a combination of oral (e.g., ivermectin) and topical (e.g., permethrin) therapy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q47

questions.question: An 87-year-old woman with dementia is clinically worsening over 4 weeks. [image-based question: pictures shown of verrucous lesions on the hands and erythematous lesions on her back]
questions.question_raw: 87yo demented woman clinically worsening over 4 weeks. [image-based question: pictures shown of verrucous lesions on the hands and erythematous lesions on her back]
questions.model_answer: a) Crusted (Norwegian) scabies. Psoriasiform hyperkeratotic/verrucous crusted papular lesions of the hands (with scalp, face, neck, feet and nail involvement) in an institutionalized, demented older adult is the classic presentation, driven by high mite burden from impaired immunity and inability to comply with care.

questions.question: Scabies.

parts_raw.text: A. List two infection control measures

questions.model_answer:
(1) Contact precautions with gown and gloves — required for crusted (Norwegian) scabies and used for classic scabies during direct skin contact — continued until 24 hours after effective scabicidal therapy; for crusted scabies place in a single room with dedicated equipment.
(2) Environmental and contact management: launder clothing, bed linen and towels in hot water and hot dryer (or bag for 72 hours), vacuum the room, and treat household contacts and identified exposed healthcare workers prophylactically, excluding symptomatic staff from work until 24 hours after treatment.

cohort_answer.text: Typical scabies: Routine Precautions, use gloves and gown with direct patient contact. Crusted scabies: Contact Precautions. Duration of precautions: Until 24 hours after initiation of appropriate therapy. General measures: wash clothes/bedding in hot water etc. Prophylaxis: Household contacts treated; asymptomatic HCW contact with typical scabies offered scabicidal prophylaxis; asymptomatic HCW contact with crusted scabies MUST be offered prophylaxis; Symptomatic HCWs excluded from work, return 24 hrs after completing treatment

questions.question: An 85-year-old woman in a nursing home has an itchy rash on the wrists and arms; she was treated with steroids and improved, but now other residents have developed the same thing.
questions.question_raw: 85F in nursing home with itchy rash on wrists and arms, treated with steroids, gets better but then others have come down with the same thing.

parts.text: What are two infection control measures?

questions.model_answer:
a) Scabies (classic scabies vulgaris) — intensely pruritic papular rash of the finger webs and flexor wrists in an institutionalized older adult with transmission to other residents.
b) Sarcoptes scabiei (var. hominis).
c) (1) Topical 5% permethrin cream applied from the neck down and washed off after 8–14 h, with a second application after 1 week (CDC first-line). (2) Oral ivermectin 200 µg/kg single dose, repeated in 14–15 days (not ovicidal); preferred for demented/non-adherent patients who cannot comply with topical application.
d) (1) Treat the infested patient and all close/household/institutional contacts simultaneously regardless of symptoms. (2) Hot wash-dry decontamination of all clothing and bedding by machine washing and drying at ≥60°C (140°F), or disposal of contaminated items.

cohort_answer.text: Scabies. Organism: Sarcoptes scabiei var hominis. Treatments: Permethrin cream 5% (leave 8-14h); Ivermectin 200mcg/kg single oral dose, repeat after 1-2 weeks. Infection control: Contact precautions, treat everyone at same time, thorough cleaning of surfaces/bedding/clothing, dedicated care team, isolation of affected patient
